with which we deal. I am glad to see a little something by way of principle for widows, but I wish we would apply that principle in all pieces of legislation.
1 urge that throughout the whole gamut of pension arrangements the widow's pension should be the same amount as the husband would get if she had died first. I argue as well that the person who is usually referred to as a second wife-she might not be, she might be the first wife of the old chap- should get the widow's pension despite the fact she may have married him after he left the bench or retired from whatever employment he had.
1 know of cases where the so-called second marriage has lasted longer than the first. I know of many cases where in the so-called second marriage the wife had a great deal to do by way of attending to her husband in a period of illness and when the illness ended in his death, there was nothing for her. I am glad the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona said what he did in this area. It prompted the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence (Mrs. Appol-loni) to make an interjection. Salaries do increase, partly because we produce a much greater volume of goods and services and partly because of inflation. We should not always bow to the proposition that those at the top should get the increases first. If someone says this may have a bearing on what I will be saying about increases for members of Parliament when that piece of legislation is brought in, my reply is that members know where 1 stood the last few times. 1 will be taking the same stand again.
I say this about judges. They themselves should say that they could get along and could be given lesser increases than are provided in this bill. I quite agree with the member for York South-Weston, the Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence, that maybe it was a bit of an insult for the member for Edmonton-Strathcona to say that a judge would take it out on him or his wife before the courts. 1 am sure he did not mean it that way and that no judge would act that way. 1 think judges have the respect of the citizens of this country because of the positions they hold and because of their impartiality; they do not need high salaries to get respect. I am looking across the way at a friend of mine. 1 will not name him in case he does not want to own up to it, but he is one who agreed with me in the elevator the other day that position in society is not necessarily marked by the amount of salary one receives.

speechtext:
My hon. friend has identified himself and has added that we should not impose our virtue on other people. 1 do not think it is a matter of virtue. 1 think it is a matter of fairness, justice and common sense.
Let us go back to the widows of disabled veterans whose pensions were below the 48 per cent level and who have finally been accorded those pensions. Some of them must wait six and a half years. Judges' widows get it right away. I think of the people who are waiting, and who keep waiting, for salary increases. I find in this bill the increases are to be retroactive.
There are two stages of retroactivity but they will be retroactive whenever the bill is passed. As I read the bill, a judge who may have retired will still get the increase for the time he was on the bench, which is quite different from what happens to employees of the public service when there is an increase in salaries; it goes only to those who are on staff at the time it comes into effect.
I am just pleading for some fair play and justice in the whole thing. 1 know the arguments in defence of salaries as
high as $88,000 a year. That is a lot of money. Ian Sinclair of the Canadian Pacific Railway receives a lot more than that.

The only way we found out the amount of his salary was because the parent people in the United States had to reveal the information down there.
The other day one of my friends mentioned how much school teachers make compared with what members of Parliament make. I said, "Which do you want to be?" He did not hesitate for a moment. He said he would rather be in Parliament. 1 still believe there is some sense to Edward Bellamy's concept in "Looking Backward" when he suggested that the people who do the meanest, hardest and dirtiest work should be paid or compensated for it because those who are doing the kind of work we are engaged in have far more satisfaction in doing it. Now the hon. member is shaking his head, no doubt in disbelief.

speechtext:
It seems to me the satisfaction that judges, members of Parliament and others get out of their jobs should be taken into account. We do not always have to put them first. There are too many people out there today wrestling with the prices of butter, milk, bread, tea and coffee, prices the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) had to admit the other day he did not even know. These people worry from day to day. People are having to renegotiate their mortgages at 16 per cent, 17 per cent, 18 per cent and 20 per cent and are worrying about how far things will go. Yet, we can do what is in this bill, make it all retroactive and tidy it up.
There is something about all of this I want to propose, and 1 am going to propose it particularly in relation to the pension provisions in this bill. It has often been suggested in the House of Commons, when dealing with procedural matters and so on, that the practice we have of governments bringing in legislation in its final form, meaning that all the House can do is accept it or reject it, is not sacred. Maybe there are times when members of the House of Commons should have some input before a bill is put in its final form. We have done that a few times. We did it with respect to the National Transportation Act a few years ago; we have done it with respect to our divorce legislation and at other times as well. We have given a bill first reading and then, before it was given a second reading, had its subject matter sent off to committee so the whole thing could be looked over. This ought to be done with the bill before us. Instead of giving this bill a second reading, which is approval in principle, it would be far better if we sent the subject matter off to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs and let hon. members like the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona, the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Jarvis) and the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence have some say precisely because there are all these salary figures allowances, widows' arrangements and pension arrangements.

At the end of my remarks 1 shall seek to move an amendment to the effect that the bill not be read a second time but that we send the subject matter off to committee. I am doing this not only because 1 think there should be that kind of discussion with respect to these salaries and what we do for widows-and my friend, the hon. member for New Westmin-ster-Coquitlam would like to have something to say about how few women there are on the bench-but 1 do it particularly with respect to a major principle involving pensions contained in this bill. It is the decision of the government that judges' pensions are now to be non-contributory. 1 remember well from years ago when the pensions of judges were non-contributory and, incidentally, were paid only to the judge. I remember when judges came along to Mr. Ilsley when he was the Minister of Justice and complained there was nothing for the widow. A very happy solution was reached. The judge's pension was divided into two parts. One part was two-thirds, the other part was one-third. The two-thirds was considered as the judge's pension and the one-third was considered as the wife's pension. If she died first he lived on two-thirds of the pension and if he died first she received the third. They were all happy for a while but not happy ever after.
As they wanted better pensions, the government came in with the proposition that they should be put on a contributory basis and, on that basis, be made better off. Who was the minister who brought that into effect in 1975? None other than the person who is now the Minister of Justice. He was then the President of the Treasury Board. He proposed to put the pensions of judges on a proper basis-on the basis of a principle which was defensible-and mainly that they should be on contributory basis. Now that same individual, having been transplanted or transmigrated from the Treasury Board to the Department of Justice, says we should end the contributory principle. The argument is that it created two classes of judges-some on non-contributory pensions and some on contributory pensions. If you want to put it on the basis of equality, those who are out there should be required to pay for the pensions they received. That is a form of retroactivity which would be a bit rough. But it is really unfair to the whole public to pick out this one group of people and say "Your pensions shall be non-contributory". The bill goes even further than that. It not only proposes that from here on they shall be non-contributory, but that those judges who have contributed under the laws as applied since 1975 should get all their money back plus interest. You do not find very many examples of that in any pension plan.
I urge very strongly that that be reconsidered. I think it is too complicated for us to study here on the floor of the House of Commons, and that is why I think it should be looked at in the standing committee. The hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona objected to our sending this bill to committee on the grounds that once it gets there, it is not likely to be changed by either a comma or a semicolon, and he is right. That is why I am suggesting, not that we send the bill to the committee carved in stone, but that we send the subject matter

of the bill to the committee and let the members of that committee go over it before it is put in the final form in which it will come to this House.
I think that there are many aspects of the bill which should be considered, but I think that non-contributory pension provisions should be considered very carefully before they are put before us as something on which to vote in its final form. I believe that many members feel that way. I think the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona in that part of his speech speaks not just for himself but for a number of members in his own party, and I suspect that he and I are speaking for a number of Liberal members on the other side of the House as well. All of the other pension plans in this country are on a contributory basis. The only one I can think of that is not is the pension of the Governor General and the special pension for a prime minister who has been in office for four years. Poor Joe did not make it. There is some defence for that. The Governor General's salary was fixed in the British North America Act way back to begin with, and increasing it has apparently been difficult. The Prime Minister, of course, has provided a rather generous pension for governors general, but the present Governor General, before he took office, said he wants that act amended so that if he leaves that job before he reaches the age of 50, he would not get the pension at that point but it would be deferred until a later date. I believe the Prime Minister promised Mr. Schreyer, before he took the office, that this would be done, but he did want to look at something to protect his widow in case anything happened to Mr. Schreyer while he was Governor General. With these exceptions, and no doubt there are some others, I have no doubt there are big corporations which provide-

be changed in committee, given the opinions voiced on all sides of the House.
The government House leader is present in the House. He knows 1 have spoken with him privately about that aspect of the pensions. It is the part which really concerns me, and I pass that comment to him. He has made no comment to me with respect to it, and I do not suggest that the hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi is speaking for the government House leader or for the government. But, it is an indication of support on the government side of the House with respect to a concern which we share as well. We should all take it into account when considering the amendment of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
I would not engage myself in this debate if I did not think it was important. A number of opinions were expressed in the House about judges on December 1 and today. As the Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development (Mr. Chretien) said, sometimes we forget that there is a peculiar responsibility in the Parliament of Canada respecting the appointment of judges to ensure that the emoluments are sufficient to invite or entice the best in the profession to accept an appointment to the bench and not cast some doubt on the independence of judges because their emoluments, salaries and benefits may not be acceptable, having regard to modern day standards in the profession.
We must remember that judges are peculiar. While they are a special class of people by virtue of their work, they are also a special class of Canadians in the sense that when a federally-appointed judge accepts a position on the bench, he loses some of his most fundamental civil rights. He loses the right to speak publicly on a matter of public interest, even with respect to the operation of his own court except in a most peripheral manner. He loses the right to vote; he cannot choose his member of Parliament.
Indeed there is some doubt as to whether he can even approach his member of Parliament. Given that set of circumstances, this Parliament or any Parliament owes a particular duty to those individuals who accept that special brand of public service to treat them appropriately, but not overly kindly or meanly. We should not talk about them meanly because they cannot speak for themselves. It is important to remember that.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said something in the course of his speech to which I listened and which verified by asking someone else. He admitted that the judges should have some increase, but his quarrel seemed to be with respect to the amount. He thought the package being offered to judges was a bit rich in the circumstances.

I see the hon. member nodding his head. It is a matter of opinion. I was the member of a government which considered the question of the pay package for federally-appointed judges. While the pay package we proposed during the life of our government was somewhat less than this one, I think it could be argued, if one wished to do so,
Judges Act
that there has been a passage of time and that perhaps some adjustment should have been made to it.
But I say to my friends in the House that it is not a matter of principle; it is a matter of degree. When this bill goes to committee, as it is bound to, that issue will be discussed and evidence will be heard which I hope will move the minds of right-thinking members one way or the other as to whether the pay package should go up or down. I have to be honest with this court, the highest court in the land. I do not think the pay package is inappropriate. I am not prepared to quibble with $1,000, $2,000, $3,000 or having it stretched over three years. The fact of the matter is that judges, because of circumstances in this place and other places, have not received an increase, especially when we consider what most of them could earn outside. It is very difficult to arrive at a differential.
The principle which I try to apply in my own mind is that the pay package, the emoluments or the salaries of judges or their families ought to be such that they do not become an attraction for persons to accept appointments to the bench or a deterrent to persons accepting that particular public office. It is a difficult standard.
Another aspect is the independence of the judiciary. It is absolutely important to ensure that Her Majesty's judges are independent, that their minds are not moved by any other consideration than doing their jobs. They sit alone and judge the freedom of subjects, or whether one wins or loses a lawsuit or a dispute between two citizens. I do not know of any higher form of public service, including this House, which casts a greater responsibility on one individual than the responsibility which is cast upon a judge. Given that position, given the position we had when my party formed the government in Canada, and from what I know is happening in the United States, from discussions I have had with officials there with respect to their position, there is some difficulty in attracting the best people to the bench. And government justice ministers must make choices. I know that money will not be the complete attraction to the bench. Of course it will not be. But it ought not to be the deterrent to the excellence which we want to have on the bench. That is the principle which ought to guide us when we are considering this bill.
The hon. member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) in the course of his speech-some of which I enjoyed and some of which I say with respect to him was somewhat unfortunate-talked about the appointing process of judges. He said there was something wrong with a political party's minister of justice, who must belong to a political party, whether mine or someone clse's, making appointments to the bench and that those appointments might be questioned because they might have a partisan ring to them. In other words, a person who has been prominent in the community may be known as a Liberal or a Conservative. That is always a problem. That is the great responsibility which falls on successive ministers of justice in this country, certainly since we have been in confederation. I think generally ministers of justice over the years, whether of

the party which now forms the government or my own party, have been very conscious of the importance of attracting the best men and women to the bench-the best that were available. 1 think the court has excelled itself with the federally-appointed judges, which is what we are talking about now. They have excelled themselves and excelled even the expectation of some of their staunchest supporters in their sense of fairness, justice, impartiality and in the unbiased attitude which they have brought to their work. 1 do not think there is anything terribly wrong with our process. I do not think there is anything wrong with the minister of justice consulting with the Canadian Bar Association. And I say "consulting" the Canadian Bar Association. 1 do not think there is anything particularly wrong with the minister of justice consulting the community in which the judge has practised before being considered for an appointment. I think that is appropriate. It is like everything else, it is a judgment call which the minister of justice makes when the invitation is put forward or an application to serve is accepted. I think that kind of discussion must go on.
The fact of the matter is our system has thrown up some fine judges. Our system has also thrown up judges who were not so fine. There used to be a story that every time 1 lost a case 1 always thought there was something wrong with the judge and when I won a case I thought the judge was a fine man, that he had a wonderful legal mind. In any event, our system has thrown up some pretty good judges. It is a fine judicial system which ranks with the best in the world. We want to make sure it continues to rank with the best in the world.
